itineraries.title: Oulu in 3 Days: Hailuoto Island and Liminka Bay
itineraries.subtitle: In 3 days, explore Oulu and its Tiima museum, Hailuoto Island via its road across the sea, and Liminka Bay.
itineraries.notes: Since June 29, 2026, Hailuoto has been accessible by an 8.4 km road across the sea, and the ferry no longer runs. The Turkansaari Open-Air Museum opens only in summer (May 31 to August 30 in 2026), and Marjaniemi Lighthouse is open for daily visits only from late June to early August.
itineraries.climate: Best time to visit: mid-June to mid-August, with average afternoon temperatures of 18 to 21 °C in June, July, and August. In May and September, highs are around 13 °C, and several museums have reduced hours or are closed. Around Midsummer, daylight lasts 22 hours: bring a sleep mask and a windbreaker for Hailuoto’s shores.

visits.text: Red wooden warehouses, a bronze statue, and waterfront stalls: welcome to Kauppatori, Oulu’s market square. The old warehouses now house bars, restaurants, and craft shops. The Toripolliisi statue, the “market policeman,” was unveiled in 1987. Standing 2.2 m tall, it honors the officers who once patrolled the square. Start here: the Rotuaari pedestrian street begins just behind the statue.

In 1901, the city brought its butchers under one roof, marking the birth of Kauppahalli, Oulu’s market hall. Architects Karl Lindahl and Walter Thomé designed it in the Gothic Revival style, drawing on the forms of medieval buildings. A major renovation, completed in 2020, restored its original appearance. Inside, you’ll find local products, crafts, and souvenirs. Come for breakfast and try the salmon soup recommended by the tourist office.

“Pitch Island”: that is what the name Pikisaari means. This neighborhood of wooden houses is connected to the market square by a pedestrian bridge. Pitch is a black paste made from wood tar that was used to waterproof boat hulls. A pitch factory opened here in the 17th century, followed by shipyards and a sawmill. Artists and craftspeople live here today. In summer, visit the Sailor’s Home Museum (Merimiehen kotimuseo), housed in Oulu’s oldest wooden building.

Rain or shine, Oulu’s best attraction is also its newest: Tiima, a museum and science center that opened on October 9, 2026. It brings together the Tietomaa Science Center, the Oulu Museum, and VISIO, a room where images and sounds surround you. In the Masiina exhibition, you walk through an 1860s steam-powered robot factory. The factory is fictional, staged to look like a real industrial site. Then head up to the observation deck at the top of a tannery’s former water tower, about 45 m tall. Tickets cost €22 for adults and €14 for children.

Oulu Cathedral is named after a queen of Sweden, Sophia Magdalena, wife of King Gustav III. It was built in 1777, when Finland was part of the Kingdom of Sweden. The great fire of 1822 destroyed its wooden sections. Architect Carl Ludvig Engel rebuilt it using the old stone walls. The bell tower was not added until 1845. Inside, look for the portrait of Swedish historian Johannes Messenius, painted in 1611: it is the church’s most remarkable work of art. The cathedral is less than a 1 km walk from the market square.

Follow the Rotuaari pedestrian street to the small Kauppurienaukio square. Five large sculpted stones rise from the paving. This work, No.1574 Stone, is by British artist Rana Begum. Its shapes evoke glaciers and sea ice. It was installed in 2026, the year Oulu was a European Capital of Culture. It is a permanent installation. It belongs to Climate Clock, a trail of artworks about the climate, with the other pieces installed around Oulu. Allow 30 minutes, including the pedestrian street.

activities.text: You’re right in the city, yet sea trout swim up the streams of Hupisaaret to spawn. This park stretches across several small islands at the mouth of the Oulujoki, linked by bridges and dotted with old pavilions. It became a public park after the 1850s. At the northern end of the park, a fish ladder described as Finland’s longest helps fish swim upstream. It consists of a series of small stepped pools that they pass through one by one. Take a stroll here between visits: admission is free.

practical_info.tip: Migrating fish can be seen in the fish ladder from May through late October. Café Kiikku, in the park, opens only in summer.

to_next_leg.road_type: 8.4 km fixed link across the sea

visits.text: A tepee-inspired silhouette and a large window behind the altar define Hailuoto Church. Architects Irma and Matti Aaltonen completed it in 1972. It replaces a church built in 1620 that was destroyed by fire in 1968. In the entrance hall, a small museum displays objects saved from the flames. The church stands in the heart of the island’s main village: visit it first before driving west toward Marjaniemi.

If you’re on the island on a summer weekend, set aside 1 hour for the Kniivilä Museum (Kniivilän kotiseutumuseo). Records of this farm date back to the 1600s. Its last residents were three unmarried siblings, and the interior has been preserved almost exactly as they left it. You’ll see more than 3,000 objects, a shoemaker’s workshop, a cowshed, and a small smoke sauna with no chimney. Since 2024, the exhibition “Meren sylissä” (In the Arms of the Sea) has told the story of the island and its inhabitants. Admission is €5 and free for visitors under 18; card payments only.

The name of the Ojakylä windmill, Hyväntuulen mylly, is a play on words. In Finnish, “tuuli” means both “wind” and “mood”: this is both the mill of fair winds and the mill of good spirits. This traditional windmill is surrounded by old grain storehouses and a large cogwheel. According to local tradition, women turn it every summer to obtain a good grain harvest in the fall. An old sign on the main road points the way, and parking is available.

Your voice echoes back amplified beneath Organum’s three concrete domes in Ulkokarvo. This sound art installation tunes each dome to its own resonant frequency. This is the pitch at which the enclosed air vibrates most readily: a sound close to that pitch is amplified and sustained. Step inside a dome to sing, speak, or play an instrument. Spend a moment in silence, too, listening to the surrounding sounds.

Marjaniemi Lighthouse has watched over Hailuoto’s western tip since 1871. This 25 m brick tower, designed by architect Axel Hampus Dalström, is described as Finland’s best-preserved brick lighthouse. It still guides boats, so visits are guided, last 15 minutes, and take place in groups of about 5 people. A narrow spiral staircase with 110 steps leads to the top. Admission costs €10, with no reservations. In 2026, the lighthouse was open daily from 12 p.m. to 3 p.m., June 19 to August 9.

activities.text: Since June 29, 2026, a ferry has no longer been needed to reach Hailuoto Island. The fixed link, an 8.4 km road made up of two bridges and a causeway, starts at Riutunkari on the mainland. The crossing takes about 8 minutes. The former ferry took 25 to 30 minutes, and in summer, the wait in line could last hours. Hailuoto is the largest island in the Bothnian Bay, the northern part of the Gulf of Bothnia. It has fewer than 1,000 residents. Drive slowly on the island: there are many cyclists.

practical_info.tip: The ferry made its final crossing on June 29, 2026: the old crossing schedules no longer apply.

activities.text: At Kirkkosalmi, a reed-covered lake occupies what was once an inlet of the sea. The land on Hailuoto is rising by about 1 cm per year. The Earth’s crust, long compressed by the weight of glaciers, has been slowly rebounding since they melted. This is how the lake became cut off from the sea. Its wheelchair-accessible observation tower offers views of cormorants and birds of prey in spring.

practical_info.tip: Best time to visit: April and May, during the spring migration.

activities.text: Follow the trail’s old yellow markers to the Keskiniemi pooki on Hailuoto’s northern coast. A pooki is a daymark: a landmark built on the coast that sailors can see from a distance to determine their position. Completed in 1858, this one warned ships of the sandbanks north of the headland. It is the island’s oldest surviving daymark. The Finnish Transport Infrastructure Agency restored it in the fall of 2024.

practical_info.tip: Park in the widened area at the end of the gravel road Karvontie or Sunilahentie, then continue on foot.

activities.text: On an almost flat island, Hyypänmäki offers the most beautiful forest walk. This ridge of pine trees and sandy slopes rises to about 31 m, making it Hailuoto’s highest point. Its easy trails start at the Hyypä ski lodge. According to local tradition, the Piilopirtti gorge, “the hidden cabin,” served as a refuge during the Great Northern War (1700–1721). The war pitted Sweden, which Finland was then part of, against Russia. Look for the Hyypä scenic bench, too, a work created by local residents.

practical_info.tip: The trails are open year-round and suitable for families.

activities.text: If the wind is strong, stroll through the narrow lanes of the fishing village of Marjaniemi. Its small cabins cluster together for shelter from the wind blowing in from the sea. The village is mostly active in summer, but its harbor remains one of Bothnian Bay’s important fishing ports. Around the lighthouse, wooden boardwalks cross dunes and sandy beaches protected as natural areas. Facing west, the headland is a good place to watch the sun set over the sea.

practical_info.tip: In Marjaniemi, park only in designated parking lots (the Sumppu area, the harbor, and near the lighthouse): roadside parking is prohibited.

to_next_leg.road_type: Hailuoto fixed link to the mainland

visits.text: More than 200 bird species are spotted each year in Liminganlahti Bay (Liminka Bay), and about 160 nest there. The visitor center (Liminganlahden luontokeskus) explores their lives in the exhibition “The Eight Seasons of the Bird Year,” designed for all ages. The bay covers more than 12,000 ha. Since 2004, it has been on the Ramsar List, which identifies wetlands of international importance. Borrow binoculars for adults or children at the reception desk. In summer, the center opens as early as 8 a.m.

activities.text: Follow the 600 m gravel path, accessible to wheelchairs and strollers, to the Virkkula birdwatching tower. This two-level tower, with a covered lower level, overlooks coastal meadows: grasslands beside the sea where animals graze in summer. In spring, look for ruffs, shorebirds whose males display to attract females.

practical_info.tip: In May and June, stay on the trails: many birds nest in the coastal meadows.

activities.text: Sheep graze along the Rantaniitty trail, whose name means “shore meadow.” This 650 m gravel trail starts in the visitor center’s courtyard and is suitable for strollers. Grazing maintains the meadow. Without livestock or mowing, reeds take over, and the birds that nest in these grasslands lose their habitat. Near the center, the Kukkala garden showcases plants from the bay’s shores.

practical_info.tip: The trails are not maintained in winter.

visits.text: Nearly 50 buildings and structures spread across islands in the Oulujoki River make up the Turkansaari Open-Air Museum, about 16 km from downtown Oulu. The Ylikärppä farmyard shows rural life in the 1900s. The Parttuainen logging cabin tells the story of the men who cut timber after the war, then floated it downriver to sawmills. The museum opens only in summer: in 2026, from May 31 to August 30, 10 a.m. to 5 p.m. Admission is €12 and free for those under 18.

The most beautiful story at the Turkansaari museum begins with a simple cross drawn on a map from 1797. It marked a prayer house on the island, which was then deserted. Excavations uncovered its foundations in the early 1920s. The building itself, built in 1694 for fishermen, had been sold in 1814 and was being used as a warehouse in Oulu. It was brought back to the island in 1922, then consecrated as a church in 1925. Visit it first: the museum began with this church.

activities.text: Watch for smoke from the tar pit: every summer, the Turkansaari museum demonstrates how wood tar was made. Pine wood was burned slowly in a pit to extract the tar. It was used to waterproof wooden sailing ships. In the 19th century, Oulu was the world’s leading tar-exporting port. The Turkansaari café serves traditional Finnish snacks during opening hours.

practical_info.tip: Tar making takes place only on certain days: check the events calendar. Admission costs €2 more on event days.

visits.text: The Tähtitorni café, on the islet of Linnansaari, sits atop a gunpowder magazine from Oulu Castle. The castle was built in 1590 on an island in the Oulujoki delta. On July 31, 1793, lightning caused another gunpowder store to explode, almost completely destroying the castle. Only ruins remain. In 1875, the school for sea captains built an observatory on the surviving gunpowder magazine, hence the name Tähtitorni, “the observatory.” The café has been here since 1912. Its basement houses a small exhibition about the castle.

activities.text: If the sky is clear, end the day at Nallikari Beach, known for its sunsets over the sea. The nearby tower, called “Nallikari Lighthouse,” is actually an observation tower built in 1988, with free admission. Oulu is close enough to the Arctic Circle that around June 21, the sun dips only about 1° below the horizon. Nights stay light, and daylight lasts 22 hours.

practical_info.tip: Bike paths connect downtown to Nallikari via Pikisaari.

seo.h1_title: Oulu in 3 Days: Hailuoto Island and Liminka Bay
seo.intro_paragraph: This 3-day trip starts in Oulu, a European Capital of Culture in 2026, and explores the surrounding area by car. You spend a day and a night on Hailuoto Island, connected to the mainland by a road across the sea since June 2026. You then watch birds at Liminka Bay and visit the Turkansaari Open-Air Museum before spending your final evening in Oulu.

itineraries.title: Ostrobothnia in 4 Days: Vaasa, Kvarken, and Wooden Towns
itineraries.subtitle: In 4 days, travel from Kristinestad to Kokkola via Vaasa, the Kvarken Archipelago, and Jakobstad’s wooden district.
itineraries.notes: Start on a Tuesday: Vaasa’s museums open Wednesday through Saturday, and those in Jakobstad and Kokkola are closed on Mondays. Several sites, including the Lebell house, the Meteoria center, and the Jakobstad shipyard, open mainly from June through August.
itineraries.climate: Aim for June, July, or August: average highs in Vaasa range from 18 to 21 °C, and the summer museums are open. In May and September, expect daytime highs of 13 to 14 °C and reduced opening hours; in winter, highs stay below 0 °C. Bring a windbreaker for the archipelago and be prepared for rain in August and September, the wettest months.

visits.text: A slightly leaning, shingle-clad bell tower crowns Ulrika Eleonora Church in the heart of Kristinestad. Shingles are small wooden boards laid like roof tiles. This red wooden church was completed in 1700. Its predecessor was destroyed by lightning in 1697. Inside, look for the model ships: these are votive offerings, objects donated to the church as an expression of devotion. The church is used mainly in summer for services and weddings, so visit during that season, when it is most likely to be open.

If you visit just one interior in Kristinestad, choose the Lebell merchant’s house (Lebellska köpmansgården). Its furnished rooms show how a wealthy merchant family lived from the 1760s to the 1840s. The house dates from 1761 and became a museum in 1939. In 2026, it is open from June 1 to August 16, from 11 a.m. to 5 p.m. on weekdays and from 11 a.m. to 2 p.m. on weekends; admission costs €5.

Kristinestad’s maritime museum (Sjöfartsmuseet) occupies the attic where ships’ sails were once sewn, on the market square. It tells the story of the town’s seafaring, boatbuilding, and shipowners—the people who owned the vessels. A second exhibition room at 62 Strandgatan displays models of the town and its shipyards in the 18th and 19th centuries. In summer, the main museum opens Tuesday through Saturday, from 10 a.m. to 2 p.m.

activities.text: You will explore Kristinestad’s old town on foot. Founded in 1649, it was named after Queen Christina of Sweden. Nearly 300 wooden houses and outbuildings are protected here. Shipowners lived near the sea; the farther you get from the water, the smaller the houses become. Slip into Kattpiskargränd, which a sign describes as Finland’s narrowest two-way street. Near the church, two customs buildings dating from 1680 and 1720 recall the days when people paid a customs duty on entering town.

practical_info.tip: Kristinestad is about 1 hour 15 minutes south of Vaasa and its airport by car. The tourist office offers guided tours in several languages.

visits.text: A plain of flat fields south of Vaasa is also a crater: Söderfjärden is the depression left by a meteorite impact hundreds of millions of years ago. It measures more than 5 km across. Land uplift raised it out of the sea, then pumps drained it for farming. The Meteoria center displays meteorites from around the world; in 2026, it was open daily from June 21 to August 9 (€10).

activities.text: If you visit in September, climb the Söderfjärden observation tower near the Munsmo pumping station. According to the city of Vaasa, this is where Finland’s largest gatherings of common cranes occur: more than 7,000 birds in the fall. In spring, from late March through May, the plain also attracts many migratory birds. Bring binoculars, as the plain is vast.

practical_info.tip: There is a parking lot at the foot of the tower, with five additional spaces provided along the road for birdwatchers.

visits.text: Visit the Ostrobothnian Museum (Pohjanmaan museo) before heading to the Kvarken Archipelago. Its Terranova exhibition explains land uplift and showcases coastal wildlife: seals, migratory birds, and the nest of a white-tailed eagle, a large sea eagle. A simulator shows the ridges of stones a glacier leaves behind as it melts. Another room traces Vaasa’s history up to the 1920s. The museum opens Wednesday through Sunday, from 10 a.m. to 5 p.m.; admission costs €15 and is free for visitors under 18.

Three painters created the altarpieces in Vaasa’s Holy Trinity Church. An altarpiece is the large painting placed behind the altar. Here, they are by Albert Edelfelt, R. W. Ekman, and Louis Sparre. Edelfelt belongs to the Golden Age of Finnish art, from around 1880 to 1910. The English Gothic church was inaugurated in 1869, in the city rebuilt after the fire of 1852. Visit outside service times: allow about 20 minutes.

The Kuntsi Museum of Modern Art occupies the former customs house on the waterfront at Vaasa’s Inner Harbor. Opened in 2007, it brings together two collections of modern and contemporary art. The first comes from the foundation established by Simo Kuntsi. The second was assembled by collector Lars Swanljung and donated to the city in 2018. It opens Wednesday through Saturday, from 10 a.m. to 5 p.m. The market square is just a few minutes away on foot.

Small in size, the Tikanoja Art Museum is worth a detour for its French paintings from the 19th and early 20th centuries. It occupies the house, completed in the early 1860s, where businessman Frithjof Tikanoja settled in 1918. The house became an art museum in 1951. Older Finnish art is also on display. The museum opens Wednesday through Saturday, from 10 a.m. to 5 p.m.; it is closed Sunday through Tuesday.

In 1852, a fire devastated the wooden town of Vaasa: only 24 of its 379 private houses survived. The city was rebuilt 7 km to the northwest. In Old Vaasa (Vanha Vaasa), you will see the ruins of the stone-built St. Mary’s Church and the former court of appeal building dating from 1775, which became Korsholm Church. Look for the old stone quays, too: they now stand on dry land because the ground has risen. The Old Vaasa Museum is free and opens Wednesday through Saturday from May through August.

activities.text: You can pick up picnic supplies at Vaasa’s market hall (Kauppahalli), right in the city center. Its first hall opened on January 1, 1902, and the second in 1927. It houses seven businesses, including a fish shop and the Wasa Konditori tearoom. Shop here for the next day: in Svedjehamn, in the archipelago, a spot by the water is set up for picnics.

practical_info.tip: The €15 Ostrobothnian Museum ticket also includes same-day admission to the Kuntsi and Tikanoja museums: visit all three on a Wednesday, Thursday, Friday, or Saturday.

visits.text: Why has the Kvarken Archipelago been UNESCO-listed since 2006? The Världsarvsporten visitor center, the “World Heritage Gateway,” explains why at the foot of the Replot Bridge. During the last ice age, a layer of ice about 3 km thick pushed the ground down. Since the ice melted, the land has been rising like a mattress returning to its original shape, at about 8 mm per year. The archipelago thus gains nearly one square kilometer of land each year: this phenomenon is the main reason for its listing. Admission to the Weichsel exhibition, named after this ice age, costs €6.

activities.text: You will cross the 1,045 m Replot Bridge to reach the island of Replot from the mainland. It is a cable-stayed bridge: its deck is supported by cables stretched from two 82.5 m pylons. It was inaugurated in 1997 by the Finnish president. After visiting the center, spend some time walking along the shore. The Vaasa tourist office recommends this short walk around the bridge.

practical_info.tip: The Världsarvsporten visitor center welcomes visitors daily from 10 a.m. to 6 p.m. in June, July, and August, and from 10 a.m. to 4 p.m. in May and September. From October through April, the reception desk is staffed Monday through Thursday from 10 a.m. to 4 p.m.; the information hall and Arte Mare gallery remain open for self-guided visits during this period.

visits.text: From the top of the 20 m Saltkaret observation tower, the landscape of Svedjehamn resembles a washboard. These long, parallel ridges are De Geer moraines. They are ridges of stones and sand deposited underwater at the edge of the retreating glacier. Each is 2 to 5 m high and up to 1 km long. The tower is open year-round. A stroller-accessible path of about 1 km leads to it from the parking lot.

Red boathouses line the fishing harbor of Svedjehamn on the island of Björkö. The former fish-salting facility operated until 1989. Today it houses the Salteriet café and restaurant. You can also rent bikes there to ride along the small roads of the village of Björköby. Before leaving Vaasa, check the harbor webcam: it shows you the weather there.

activities.text: You will walk around Lake Bodvattnet on an easy trail of about 4 km, starting at Svedjehamn harbor. The path passes through Bodback, once Björkö’s main fishing harbor. As the land rose, the shoreline became too shallow for boats, and the harbor had to be moved. A few wooden boathouses and docks remain. In summer, Highland cattle, a long-haired Scottish breed, graze in the seaside meadows: keep your distance.

practical_info.tip: There is a fire pit with firewood near the Saltkaret observation tower: this is the place for your picnic.

visits.text: Skata, also known as Norrmalm, is Jakobstad’s old neighborhood of colorful wooden houses. According to the city, it is one of Finland’s largest continuous areas of historic wooden houses. Until the late 18th century, it was inhabited mainly by sailors and their families. It later became the neighborhood of workers at the Strengberg tobacco factory, the city’s largest employer around 1900. Protected since 1982, it can be explored on foot; the tourist office organizes guided tours by reservation.

Shipowner and merchant Peter Malm had Malm House (Malmska gården) built; it now houses the Jakobstad Museum. Founded in 1904, the museum focuses mainly on seafaring and shipbuilding. The name Jakobstad means “Jacob’s town.” Ebba Brahe founded it in 1652 and named it after her late husband, Jacob De la Gardie. Open Tuesday through Saturday from noon to 4 p.m.; admission €7, or €12 including the Tempus exhibition hall.

A 65 m spire marks Pedersöre Church, one kilometer south of downtown Jakobstad. Its oldest sections, built of stone, date from the 15th century. Starting in 1787, it was expanded into the shape of a cross with four equal arms. In July 1985, a fire destroyed the spire, altarpiece, and organ; the church was restored as early as 1986. The interior can only be visited by appointment; otherwise, walk around the building.

If you are traveling with children, stop at Skolparken, Jakobstad’s “school park.” This botanical garden was created in the early 20th century for schoolchildren’s botany lessons. It contains about 1,000 plant species around a pond where carp swim. Twenty minutes is enough to walk around it, between the museum and the Skata neighborhood.

Until the mid-19th century, the Old Harbor (Gamla hamn) was Jakobstad’s harbor. Its shipyard, Skeppsgården, houses two large wooden sailing ships. The Jacobstads Wapen is a replica of an 18th-century galeas, a two-masted merchant ship, built using plans from 1755. The three-masted schooner Vega was used to pay war reparations, a debt Finland owed the Soviet Union. In 2026, guided tours run from June 1 through July 31, from 10 a.m. to 4 p.m., for €15.

Nanoq means “polar bear” in Greenlandic. It is the name of Finland’s first Arctic museum, which opened in June 1991. It was founded by Pentti Kronqvist, a retired firefighter and polar explorer. In the forest near Fäboda, a main building and several small cabins tell the stories of the peoples, natural environments, and expeditions of the polar regions. From June through August, it opens Monday through Saturday from 11 a.m. to 6 p.m.; during the rest of the year, mainly on Wednesday and Thursday afternoons.

activities.text: You will end the day at Fäboda, about ten kilometers from downtown Jakobstad. Three large sandy beaches alternate with smooth rocks popular with photographers. Marked trails, ranging from a short loop to 33 km, wind through the forest, and an observation tower overlooks the shore. In the evening, settle onto the rocks to watch the sun set over the sea; there is a café near the beaches.

practical_info.tip: All three beaches have shallow water and are suitable for children. Pikkuhiekka is the busiest; the wider Isohiekka is quieter.

visits.text: The K.H. Renlund Museum is the best introduction to Kokkola’s history, and admission is free. It is named after Karl Herman Renlund, who bequeathed his art collection to the city. Roos House, built in 1813, displays about forty paintings from the golden age of Finnish art, around 1880–1910. Right next door, the Pedagogio school, completed in 1696, is Finland’s oldest wooden urban building other than a church. The museum opens Tuesday through Sunday at 11 a.m.

The British asked for it back; Kokkola kept it: an armed British naval launch is displayed in English Park (Englanninpuisto). During the Crimean War, Finland was part of the Russian Empire, which was at war with the United Kingdom. On June 7, 1854, nine British launches attacked the harbor. Soldiers and volunteers repelled them and captured this one, which still bears signs of the fighting. You can view it behind glass in its shelter in the park: allow twenty minutes.

activities.text: Look for porcelain dogs in the windows of Neristan, Kokkola’s old town. Their position indicated whether the sailor of the household was home or at sea. Some windows also have mirrors mounted outside, allowing residents to watch the street without going out. Neristan means “lower town” in Swedish. Sailors, craftspeople, and fishermen lived here, in twelve blocks of wooden houses built mainly in the 19th century. Ask Visit Kokkola for the free walking tour map, also available on your phone.

practical_info.tip: All passenger trains between Helsinki and Oulu stop at Kokkola station, and Kokkola-Pietarsaari Airport is 19 km to the south. With an extra day, you can take the M/S Jenny in summer to the lighthouse island of Tankar, 15 km offshore (June 3 through September 27 in 2026).

seo.intro_paragraph: This 4-day itinerary follows Finland’s Gulf of Bothnia coast north from Kristinestad to Kokkola. In Kvarken, you’ll see how rising land gains ground on the sea each year. You’ll then explore the old wooden neighborhoods of Jakobstad and Kokkola.

itineraries.title: Finland’s Southern Coast in 3 Days: Fiskars, Ekenäs, and Hanko
itineraries.subtitle: In 3 days, travel from the ironworks village of Fiskars to the villas of Hanko via Raseborg, Ekenäs, and the archipelago.
itineraries.notes: The boat to Jussarö, Raseborg Castle, and the Hanko Front Museum operate fully only in summer: aim for early June through late August. From Helsinki, allow about 1 hour 15 minutes to drive to Fiskars, then 1 hour 45 minutes to return from Hanko.
itineraries.climate: Best time to visit: June through August, with average highs of 17 to 21 °C in Hanko and nighttime temperatures around 10 to 14 °C. The sea stays cool, around 16 to 17 °C in July and August, and August is the rainiest month. Avoid November through March: days are very short, temperatures are often below freezing, and boats and seasonal attractions are closed.

visits.text: The village of Fiskars grew up around an ironworks in 1649. That year, Queen Christina of Sweden, who also ruled Finland at the time, authorized businessman Peter Thorwöste to produce iron here. This royal authorization had just one restriction: no cannons. Walk up the village street, lined with former ironworks buildings now used as workshops, including the copper smithy and the granary. At the top of the street, the Clock Tower Building has a Finnish clock that has kept time for the village since 1842.

Warm bread to sample in summer in the old bakery, gardening tools from bygone days on display: the Fiskars Museum (Fiskarsin museo) tells the story of ironworks workers’ lives from the 17th century to the present. Look for the pair of scissors said to be the smallest ever made in Finland. It is a reminder that the Fiskars brand is famous for its orange-handled scissors. The museum opens daily in summer and Wednesday through Sunday during the rest of the year, except in January and February.

activities.text: Set out from the village center for the Rissla Forest Trail (Risslan metsäpolku), a loop of about 4 km marked in orange. It leads to the old Rissla dam, built in 1899 along with a power plant to supply electricity to the factory. Just downstream, the stream drops about 18 m over roughly 100 m, forming a waterfall. The waterfall is fuller in spring and can almost disappear after a dry summer. The trail starts with a steep climb: bring sturdy shoes and mosquito repellent.

practical_info.tip: Start at 7 Isokiskontie, 400 m from the village parking lot. The trail is not recommended for strollers or young children.

activities.text: If you enjoy handmade objects, set aside 1 hour for the workshops in Fiskars. When the factory left the village in the 1980s, artists and craftspeople took over the empty buildings. Ceramicists, glassmakers, jewelers, and furniture makers work here today, and several open their workshops to visitors. The Fiskars shop also sells the brand’s current products, including its scissors, which are no longer made here. In summer, most shops open daily.

practical_info.tip: In fall, most shops open only Wednesday through Sunday: avoid Mondays and Tuesdays.

visits.text: A seaside castle that lost its sea: that is Raseborg Castle (Raseborgs slott), now in ruins. It was built in the 1370s on a rock surrounded by water to monitor trade in the Gulf of Finland. Since the last ice age, the land, freed from the weight of the ice, has been slowly rising. The sea therefore receded, making it increasingly difficult for boats to approach. This was one reason the castle was abandoned in the 16th century. Budget €8.50 and wear sturdy shoes: the stairs are steep.

activities.text: Walk to the Forngården Farm Museum along Lemmenpolku, the “Lovers’ Path,” a narrow forest trail about 500 m long. This open-air museum shows life on an archipelago farm in the mid-19th century. Parts of the main house date to the 18th century, and it is surrounded by a barn, storage sheds, and a smithy. On your way back, stop at Café Slottsknekten, which opened beside the ruins in 1893 to welcome tourists.

practical_info.tip: In 2026, the castle is open daily from June through August and on weekends in May, September, and October. Forngården opens Tuesday through Sunday, from 12 p.m. to 5 p.m., and its 2026 season ends on August 16.

visits.text: Gravel lanes and colorful wooden houses: Ekenäs Old Town (Gamla stan) has retained its street layout since the 16th century. King Gustav Vasa granted Ekenäs town status in 1546. Four years later, some of its merchants and craftspeople had to leave, willingly or by force, to populate a new town: Helsinki. Look for the “gossip mirrors” mounted outside windows to watch the street without being seen. The market takes place on Wednesdays and Saturdays.

The bell tower overlooking the old town belongs to Ekenäs Church (Ekenäs kyrka), a granite church completed around 1680. A fire devastated it in June 1821: only the altarpiece and a few objects were saved. Architect Charles Bassi rebuilt it between 1839 and 1842, with a roof about 10 m lower and larger windows. Inside, look at the altarpiece, the large painted panel behind the altar, made in Stockholm around 1660.

To understand Ekenäs, nothing beats 1 hour at the Raseborg Museum (Raseborgs museum). Despite its name, it is in the heart of Ekenäs: Raseborg is the municipality that has included the town since 2009. A permanent exhibition is devoted to Helene Schjerfbeck (1862–1946), one of Finland’s best-known painters. She lived in Ekenäs from 1925 to 1941 and painted many of the town’s residents. The museum is closed on Mondays and stays open until 8 p.m. on Wednesdays.

Small in size, big in architectural pedigree: Villa Skeppet (“the ship” in Swedish) is the last and smallest private house designed by Alvar Aalto, a major figure in Finnish architecture. He designed it as a gift of friendship for writer Göran Schildt and his wife Christine. In the living room, the fireplace takes the form of an abstract sculpture. Visits are by guided tour only, in English, in groups of no more than 10 people: book online (€22, about 45 minutes).

activities.text: A 15-minute walk takes you to Ramsholmen Nature Reserve, about 1 km from the center of Ekenäs. Across 55 hectares, small footbridges connect several islets covered in deciduous forest, where some trees exceed 35 m in height. In spring, wood anemones carpet the ground with flowers. A beach offers swimming in summer. The reserve is protected: dogs must stay on a leash, and fires and camping are prohibited.

practical_info.tip: Come early in the morning in spring: this is when birdsong is at its richest.

to_next_leg.road_type: Myggen III water taxi, about 1 hour 10 minutes

visits.text: Jussarö has long led sailors astray: the iron ore beneath the island pulls at compass needles, and several ships have been wrecked around its shores. This iron was mined in the 19th century, then again from the late 1950s until 1967, when falling ore prices shut the mine down. The military then used the empty buildings for urban combat training until 2005. The abandoned facilities, described as Finland’s only ghost town, occupy the eastern side of the island. Only part of the site is open to visitors.

activities.text: If you don’t have your own boat, the Myggen III water taxi takes you to Jussarö, an island in Ekenäs Archipelago National Park. Established in 1989, the park is almost 90% water. On the island, a 4.7 km nature trail passes through an old forest and alongside former ore extraction pits. Climb the observation tower where maritime pilots once watched for ships. These pilots were local sailors responsible for guiding boats between submerged rocks.

practical_info.tip: In 2026, the boat runs from June 5 to September 6: departure at 10:30 a.m. from Ekenäs North Harbor (Pohjoinen Rantakatu 12), return from Jussarö at 3 p.m., €35 round-trip, payable on board. It carries a maximum of 25 passengers, so reserve ahead.

activities.text: Red rocks and an open horizon set the scene at Iron Beach, the “iron beach,” a small beach on Jussarö. On clear days, you can watch large ships passing offshore between Finland and Sweden. Along this coast, the sea temperature is around 16 to 17 °C in July and August, making for an invigorating swim. Bring a picnic; there is a barbecue area on the island.

practical_info.tip: Drinking water is available on Jussarö. On the western side of the island, stay on the marked trail.

to_next_leg.road_type: Water taxi from Jussarö to Ekenäs Harbor, then Route 25 to Hanko
to_next_leg.justification: Segment 1: Myggen III water taxi from Jussarö to Ekenäs Harbor, about 20 km in 1 hour 10 minutes (Metsähallitus); segment 2: Route 25 from Ekenäs to Hanko, 36 km in 33 minutes; the boat is the main mode of transportation by duration, and the previous duration of 1 hour 43 minutes covered travel alone, without waiting time.

visits.text: Hanko’s most beautiful side is built of wood: the villas on its southern tip. After the spa resort opened in 1879, wealthy families, some from St. Petersburg, had villas built here with intricately crafted wooden facades. They are nicknamed “lace villas.” Most still stand around the spa park (Kylpyläpuisto) and along Bulevardi. Beside Plagen Beach, the Casino, an events hall dating from 1879, offers no gambling: it is a summer restaurant.

Between 1880 and 1930, about 250,000 Finns left their country through the port of Hanko, bound for the United States, Canada, or Australia. Hanko Museum (Hangon museo) tells their stories in its exhibition “Where the Land Meets the Sea,” which opened in 2025. It also explores life in the villas, industry, and the peninsula’s natural environment. The museum occupies a former mechanical engineering factory, with no steps or thresholds. It is open Tuesday through Friday from 10 a.m. to 6 p.m. and on weekends from 11 a.m. to 4 p.m.

Hanko Front Museum (Hangon rintamamuseo) is in Lappohja, on the road to Ekenäs, about 21 km from Hanko, a 20-minute drive. In March 1940, the peace agreement that ended the Winter War against the Soviet Union required Finland to lease the Hanko Peninsula to the Soviets for 30 years as a naval base. The base’s boundary ran about a hundred meters from the museum. The Soviets left as early as December 1941. Behind the building, a trail of about 1 km follows the trenches. Open Tuesday through Sunday from June to August, and just one day a week during the rest of the year.

activities.text: Walk to the very end of mainland Finland along the 6.7 km Tulliniemi nature trail. It crosses pine forest, dry meadows, and rounded rocks to reach Uddskatan, the point where the Gulf of Finland meets the Archipelago Sea. About half a million migrating birds pass over this point each year. Since 1979, a bird observatory has counted them and fitted numbered bands to their legs to track their journeys. The trail is for pedestrians only.

practical_info.tip: Park at 1 Vapaasatama and follow the white-topped posts. The rocks are slippery in wet weather.

activities.text: A guest book carved into rock: that is the nickname of Hauensuoli, the “pike’s gut,” a narrow channel between two islets off Tulliniemi. Sailors waiting here for favorable winds carved their names and coats of arms into the rock—the designs that served as emblems for noble families. There are more than 600 carvings, the oldest dating from the 15th century. The boat leaves from East Harbor (Itäsatama), and the trip lasts about 2 hours.

practical_info.tip: Trips run on Tuesdays and Saturdays at 2 p.m., from July 2 to August 13, 2026, depending on the weather and passenger numbers. Book through SunFun.

activities.text: Climb to the Emigrant Monument on the rocks along Merikatu, facing the sea: three cranes take flight toward the open water. An association erected it together with 93 Finnish municipalities, each of which had lost more than a tenth of its population to emigration. Continue onto Puistovuori along the “Path of Love” (Rakkauden polku), about 1.5 km long, laid out in the late 19th century for spa resort guests. Emigrants are said to have come to dance on its flat rock while waiting for their ships.

practical_info.tip: The Path of Love is a good late-afternoon walk, after visiting the Casino and the villas in the spa park.

seo.h1_title: Finland’s Southern Coast in 3 Days: Fiskars, Ekenäs, and Hanko
seo.intro_paragraph: This 3-day itinerary follows Finland’s southwestern coast, about an hour’s drive from Helsinki. You travel from a former ironworks village taken over by craftspeople to the ruins of a medieval castle, then to the wooden old town of Ekenäs. A boat then takes you to the mining island of Jussarö, before Hanko’s wooden villas and southern tip.
seo.seo_hook: Fiskars workshops, Raseborg Castle, Ekenäs old town, Jussarö island, and Hanko villas: 3 days on Finland’s southwestern coast.
featured_list: Fiskars: an ironworks village founded in 1649, now a village of craftspeople
Raseborg: a castle from the 1370s left behind by the sea
Ekenäs: a wooden old town and the Helene Schjerfbeck exhibition at Raseborg Museum
Jussarö: an abandoned mining town in a national park
Hanko: villas with intricate woodwork and Finland’s southern tip

itineraries.title: Helsinki in 2 Days: Suomenlinna, Seurasaari, and Design
itineraries.subtitle: Explore Senate Square, Suomenlinna, the major museums, and the island of Seurasaari in 2 days on foot and by ferry.
itineraries.notes: According to the 2026 opening hours, Helsinki Cathedral is closed to visitors on Saturdays, and the Old Market Hall is closed on Sundays: ideally, plan your trip for a Friday and Saturday. The Suomenlinna ferry runs year-round, but the Seurasaari Museum is only open from May 15 to September 15.
itineraries.climate: Best time to visit: June through August, with highs of 19 to 22 °C and nearly 19 hours of daylight in late June. May and September are still pleasant, at around 15 °C, and fall at either end of the Seurasaari Museum’s season. In winter, highs hover around 0 °C, and daylight lasts less than 6 hours in late December: dress warmly for the crossing to Suomenlinna.

visits.text: Senate Square (Senaatintori) is the best place to start getting to know Helsinki. Architect Carl Ludvig Engel designed the four major buildings surrounding it. The most prominent is the white Lutheran cathedral, completed in 1852 at the top of a broad flight of steps. In the center, the statue of Tsar Alexander II commemorates his reforms, which gave Finland greater autonomy when it was part of the Russian Empire. According to its 2026 opening hours, the cathedral is closed to visitors on Saturdays. Admission costs €8 from June to early November.

to_next_leg.justification: Trajet urbain fait à pied entre senaatintori et uspenskin katedraali, environ 600 m de marche réelle comptés 1 km : l'ancienne durée de 3 min venait du calcul voiture, elle est remplacée par 9 min de marche.

visits.text: Seven hundred thousand reclaimed bricks were used to build Uspenski Cathedral (Uspenskin katedraali). They came from Bomarsund, a fortress in the Åland Islands destroyed during the Crimean War, and were shipped across the sea on barges. Consecrated in 1868, the Orthodox church stands atop the hill in the Katajanokka district, east of the harbor. Inside, look at the iconostasis, the large icon-covered screen separating the altar from the congregation. Admission is €5; the cathedral is closed to visitors on Mondays. From September to April, it is open on Saturdays from 10 a.m. to 3 p.m.

activities.text: The aroma of salmon soup drifts through the aisles of the Old Market Hall (Vanha kauppahalli), beside Market Square (Kauppatori). Opened in 1889, it is the city’s oldest market hall. It is known for this soup and its fish sandwiches. Outside, stalls selling Finnish products and souvenirs become more numerous from spring through fall. In winter, heated tents still serve coffee. Eat here before catching the ferry, which departs from the edge of the square.

practical_info.tip: The Old Market Hall is open Monday through Saturday, from 8 a.m. to 6 p.m. The HSL ferry to Suomenlinna departs every 15 to 30 minutes in summer and every 40 to 60 minutes in winter, using a regular public transit ticket.

to_next_leg.road_type: HSL ferry, approximately 15 minutes for the crossing

visits.text: Follow the Blue Route, marked with blue signs, from the main pier to the King’s Gate (Kuninkaanportti). This roughly 1.5 km path crosses Suomenlinna, a sea fortress whose construction began in 1748, when Finland was part of the Kingdom of Sweden. The site has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1991. The King’s Gate marks the spot where the ship carrying King Adolf Frederick of Sweden dropped anchor in 1752 during an inspection visit. Allow 1 hour to 1 hour 30 minutes of walking, excluding stops, and wear sturdy shoes for the cobblestones.

A church that also serves as a lighthouse: that is Suomenlinna Church. It was built in 1854 for the Orthodox soldiers of the Russian garrison. It became Lutheran when Finland took control of the fortress. Its tower still guides aircraft and boats: its light emits four flashes, corresponding to the letter H in Morse code, for Helsinki. The church is on the Blue Route, and admission is charged only from June through August.

If the weather takes a turn for the worse, the Suomenlinna Museum is a good place to shelter. Open year-round, it tells the story of the fortress, its restoration, and life there today: about 800 people still live on the islands. Several other museums, including the Vesikko submarine, are only open in summer. Each museum sells its own ticket, while the ramparts and squares are free to explore. The Museokortti, an annual pass valid at 360 Finnish museums, provides admission to most of Suomenlinna’s museums.

activities.text: Esplanadi is a narrow park lined with linden trees, between Market Square and Erottaja Square. At the harbor end, the Havis Amanda fountain by sculptor Ville Vallgren dates from 1908. In the middle of the park, the statue of national poet Johan Ludvig Runeberg is the work of his own son, Walter. The Kappeli restaurant, built in 1867, occupies the end of the park nearest the market. Opposite it, Espa Stage, the park’s bandstand, hosts free concerts from May through late August.

practical_info.tip: In winter, the park remains pleasant in the evening thanks to its seasonal lights.

activities.text: Helsinki residents call the statue in the small Kolmikulma Park “Diana,” although it depicts Tellervo, the forest goddess in Finnish mythology. The Design District was founded around this triangular park in 2005, when designers and local business owners joined forces. Today, the district brings together about 200 members across 25 streets, offering ceramics, jewelry, Finnish fashion, galleries, and secondhand stores. Look for the small black logo in storefront windows: it identifies businesses that belong to the district.

practical_info.tip: Wander without a set route between Kolmikulma Park and the Design Museum, 400 m away.

visits.text: Gustaf Nyström, the architect of the Old Market Hall, also designed the Design Museum (Designmuseo) building in 1894. Today, this museum and the former Museum of Architecture together form the Museum of Architecture and Design (Arkkitehtuuri- ja designmuseo). Its collections trace Finnish design and architecture, from early classics to recent creations. It is open from 11 a.m. to 6 p.m., except on Mondays from September through May. Admission is free for visitors under 18.

visits.text: Head straight to the top floor of Oodi Central Library, nicknamed “Book Heaven.” You will find 100,000 items, reading corners, nine living trees, and a balcony facing Parliament. Oodi opened on December 5, 2018, the day before Independence Day. The national government and the city gave it to the Finnish people to mark 100 years of the country’s independence. On the middle floor, a workshop open to the public offers 3D printers and laser cutters. Admission is free, with weekend hours from 10 a.m. to 8 p.m.

visits.text: Five cone-shaped domes rise like bubbles from the ground in Lasipalatsi Square. They are the skylights of Amos Rex, an art museum that opened in 2018, with galleries built beneath the square. The museum’s address is Lasipalatsi, or “Glass Palace,” a Functionalist building from 1936 with simple lines and no ornamentation. Tickets cost €20 online, and admission is free for visitors under 18. On weekends, the museum is open from 11 a.m. to 5 p.m. It is closed on Tuesdays and during exhibition changeovers.

visits.text: Helsinki’s most surprising church is barely noticeable from the street: Temppeliaukio Church (Temppeliaukion kirkko) is carved into rock. Architect brothers Timo and Tuomo Suomalainen completed it in 1969. Its walls are cut from granite about two billion years old. Left exposed, the rock gives the space acoustics prized for concerts. Above, a copper dome rests on a ring of windows that lights the nave. Admission is €8. On Sundays, the 10 a.m. service lasts about 1 hour 30 minutes, so come after noon.

to_next_leg.justification: Trajet urbain fait à pied entre temppeliaukion kirkko et sibelius monumentti, environ 1550 m de marche réelle comptés 2 km : l'ancienne durée de 5 min venait du calcul voiture, elle est remplacée par 20 min de marche.

visits.text: The Sibelius Monument (Sibelius-monumentti) brings together 569 welded steel pipes in Sibelius Park, by the sea. Created by sculptor Eila Hiltunen, it was unveiled in 1967 in tribute to composer Jean Sibelius. This abstract sculpture caused an uproar: some critics saw it as nothing more than an organ. To calm the debate, a portrait of the composer was added to a nearby granite wall. Step inside the structure: the pipes reverberate with echoes.

to_next_leg.justification: Trajet urbain fait à pied entre sibelius monumentti et seurasaari, environ 2050 m de marche réelle comptés 2 km : l'ancienne durée de 4 min venait du calcul voiture, elle est remplacée par 26 min de marche.

visits.text: “Finland in miniature”: that was the vision for Seurasaari Museum (Seurasaaren ulkomuseo), an open-air museum founded in 1909. On this wooded island, 89 wooden buildings have been relocated from across Finland: farmhouses, a parsonage, manor houses, and a windmill. The oldest date from the late 17th century. The museum is open from May 15 to September 15, from 11 a.m. to 5 p.m. Tickets cost €14, and admission is free for visitors under 18. Through the end of August, the 3 p.m. guided tour in English is included in the ticket.

activities.text: You will cross Seurasaari’s white wooden bridge, where ducks, swans, and geese await walkers. The island is free to visit year-round, with a loop of about 3.1 km along sandy paths. Its red squirrels are used to visitors and often come close. To return downtown, bus 24 serves the island, and tram 4 stops at Paciuksenkatu, about 1 km away on foot.

practical_info.tip: From mid-September to mid-May, the museum’s houses remain closed, but the island’s paths stay open for walks.

seo.h1_title: Helsinki in 2 Days: Suomenlinna, Seurasaari, and Design
seo.intro_paragraph: This 2-day weekend in Helsinki is done entirely on foot and by ferry. The first day connects Senate Square, Uspenski Cathedral, the harbor market, Suomenlinna Fortress, and the design district. The second takes you to Oodi Library, Amos Rex Museum, the church carved into rock, and Seurasaari Museum, an open-air museum.
seo.seo_hook: Helsinki in 2 days without a car: Suomenlinna Fortress, a church carved into rock, Oodi Library, design, and Seurasaari Open-Air Museum.
